The mockup jet aircraft model is 14.5 m long, 9.42 m wide, and 4.5 m high.
The aircraft includes a dielectric radome and thin lossy coatings of uniform thickness 1.5 mm on wings and tail stabilizers.
The IE–DDM decomposes the aircraft model into 13 geometrical groups and further into 45 subdomains for computation.
The combined field integral equation (CFIE) formulation is used to avoid internal resonance issues.
Robin-type transmission conditions are employed to enforce continuity of tangential fields across subdomain interfaces.
Nonconformal meshes at subdomain interfaces are handled by creating union meshes for accurate numerical integration.
The method integrates a generalized combined field integral equation (G-CFIE) for penetrable dielectric targets.
A specialized finite-element–boundary-element (FEBE) method models PEC targets coated with lossy thin materials.
The coupling parameter in CFIE is set to 0.5 to balance electric and magnetic field operators.
Surface currents on subdomain interfaces are expanded using Rao–Wilton–Glisson (RWG) basis functions.
The resulting discretized system is solved using a preconditioned Krylov subspace iterative method with a block-Jacobi preconditioner.
The multilevel fast multipole algorithm (MLFMA) accelerates the coupling of subdomains.
The method enables independent meshing of subdomains, simplifying mesh generation for multiscale features.
The scattered fields from other subdomains act as secondary incident waves in the domain decomposition iteration.
The approach allows full-wave electromagnetic scattering solutions for electrically large and multiscale composite targets.
The paper presents numerical results demonstrating the method's capability on a complex jet aircraft model at X-band frequencies.
The integral operators L and K represent electric and magnetic field integral operators respectively, based on Stratton–Chu formulas.
Transmission conditions ensure that the tangential electric and magnetic fields are continuous across interfaces despite nonmatching meshes.
The method addresses the 'mixed-frequency' problem caused by coexistence of electrically large and small features.
The domain decomposition approach reduces the ill-conditioning of the global matrix equation arising from multiscale geometry.
